notes.meaning: Sailors and merchants travel far out onto the open ocean to do business. Ancient people saw the sea as very dangerous, but those traveling for honest work can trust in God's care.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church theologian Augustine understood the deep waters as a symbol for many different nations of people.

notes.meaning: People who travel by ship see the wonders of God's creation in ways land-dwellers never do. They experience the vastness of the ocean, the variety of sea creatures, and the power of great storms.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the deep waters as a picture of the human heart, which can be hidden and full of unseen depths.

notes.meaning: God commands the weather, and a fierce wind begins to blow. The powerful gales churn up the sea and create massive waves.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw this storm as a picture of conflict and division shaking the church like a boat on rough waters.

notes.meaning: The ship climbs to the top of giant waves and then drops steeply into deep ocean troughs. The extreme danger terrifies everyone on board, and their courage completely melts away.
The deck tosses so wildly that the sailors stumble and fall like people who are drunk. Every skill and trick they know fails them, leaving them helpless and without hope.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied this to church teachers whose human wisdom can fail when deep trials arrive.

notes.meaning: Having exhausted all their own efforts, the crew calls out to the Lord for rescue. God hears their desperate prayers and saves them from their deadly situation.
God speaks and commands the roaring winds to settle down into a quiet breeze. The crashing waves become calm and still at His command.
The sailors are filled with joy when the terrifying noise stops and the waters grow peaceful. God then steers their ship safely into the harbor they were longing to reach.

Those who have been rescued are called to thank God for His unfailing love and wonderful protection. They should praise Him not only in private, but also in front of the whole congregation and before town leaders.
God can dry up flowing rivers and turn lush, fertile ground into a barren, salty wasteland. He brings about this judgment when the people living there persistently practice evil.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note this verse may point to the destruction of the Canaanites, whose wickedness brought ruin to their land.

notes.meaning: In His mercy, God can also do the exact opposite by pouring water into a parched desert. He turns dry ground into gushing springs and pools of water.
God brings hungry and needy people into this newly watered land to make a home. There they find a place of rest and are able to build a city.
The settlers work the soil, planting fields of grain and vineyards. God rewards their honest labor with rich harvests year after year.
God gives them His blessing, causing their families to multiply and their communities to grow. He also protects their farm animals so that their herds continue to thrive.
At other times, a prosperous group can be brought low through cruelty, foreign rule, and deep sorrow. God allows hardship to remind people of their weakness and their need for Him.
God brings disgrace upon proud, tyrannical rulers and strips them of their power. He leaves them wandering aimlessly in a barren wilderness where there is no path.
While God humbles the proud, He rescues the poor from their suffering. He lifts them out of misery and blesses them with large, peaceful families like flocks of sheep.
Righteous people see God's fair rule and rejoice in His goodness. Those who love evil are completely silenced, having nothing left to say against God's justice.
Anyone who is truly wise will pay close attention to these patterns in life and history. By watching God's actions, believers learn how rich and steady His faithful love really is.
